seoTitle: How to Write a Book in Google Docs (2026)
metaDescription: Structure a manuscript in Google Docs: page setup, heading styles, page breaks, a table of contents, named versions, and the native EPUB export most self-publishing platforms expect.
intro: Turning scattered notes into a structured, publication-ready manuscript is much easier with the right Google Docs setup from day one. Retrofitting structure onto 60,000 words later is painful. The tools that matter most for a book-length project — page setup, heading styles, page breaks, and named versions — are ones most people never touch in a short document. This guide walks through configuring each one using a real sample manuscript as the working example, so you can see what a properly structured chapter looks like.

steps.heading: Name your file and pick a working title
steps.body: Open a new Google Doc and rename it from Untitled document to your working title right away. Google Docs autosaves continuously, so there's no separate "create project" step, but naming the file early keeps it easy to find in Drive once you have a dozen other documents open. Treat this file as your single master copy, not a set of separate chapter documents. Splitting chapters apart is what breaks the outline and table of contents features you'll rely on later.

steps.heading: Configure your page size and margins
steps.body: Click File, then Page setup, to open the dialog controlling paper size, orientation, margins, and even a page color if you're formatting for a specific print trim size. The margins here default to 1 inch on all sides, which works for a standard manuscript, but if you're targeting a specific print size you can switch the Paper size dropdown away from the default and adjust from there. You can also apply these settings to just the selected content rather than the whole document, which is useful if your front matter needs different margins than your chapters.

image.caption: The Page setup dialog, with Apply to set to Selected content, Portrait orientation, A4 paper size, a page color swatch, and 1-inch margins on all four sides.

steps.heading: Build a proper title page
steps.body: On your first page, type your book's title and apply the Heading 1 style so it's visually distinct from everything else in the manuscript, then add a subtitle line beneath it in regular text. A cover image or hero graphic can sit right below the title if you want the front matter to feel like a finished book instead of a plain draft. This page becomes the first entry in your outline once you've applied that heading, which is what lets you jump straight back to it later.

image.caption: A title page reading "The Lantern Keeper" in Heading 1 style, with a subtitle line and a full-width image beneath it, and a page indicator on the right showing pagination is active.

steps.heading: Style every chapter heading consistently
steps.body: For each new chapter, type the title, something like "Chapter 1: The Last Light", and apply a consistent heading style throughout, whether that's Heading 1 for every chapter or Heading 3 if chapters sit beneath a higher-level part or section heading. Consistency matters more than which level you pick: mixing heading levels randomly across chapters is what breaks the outline navigation and the table of contents later, so decide on a scheme early and stick to it for the whole manuscript.

image.caption: A chapter opening with its title styled as a heading in the toolbar, followed by the body paragraphs of the scene.

steps.heading: Insert page breaks so chapters start fresh
steps.body: Place your cursor at the very end of a chapter, click Insert in the top menu, hover over Break, and select Page Break. This forces the next chapter to start at the top of a new page instead of continuing partway down the previous one, which is standard in any printed or exported book. Page breaks only work in the regular "pages" view; if your document is set to pageless format, switch it back under File, then Page setup, before inserting one. The same Insert menu is also where you'll find Table for structured content, Chart if you're including data, and Building blocks or Smart chips for anything more dynamic than plain prose.

image.caption: The Insert menu open, showing Table, Building blocks, Smart chips, Chart, and Break — the Break submenu is where Page Break lives.

steps.heading: Use the Document Outline to navigate
steps.body: Click the outline icon in the top-left corner of the page to open the Document Outline sidebar, which lists every heading you've applied as a clickable link. In a manuscript running dozens of pages, this becomes your primary way of moving around: clicking a chapter title in the outline jumps you straight there instead of scrolling through everything in between.

steps.heading: Add a table of contents and save named versions
steps.body: In your front matter, click Insert, then Page elements, then Table of contents, and choose a layout. It builds itself from your headings and updates as you add, rename, or reorder chapters. As you hit meaningful milestones, click Last edit near the top right, pick a version, open the More menu, and choose Name this version to freeze a checkpoint you can return to later. That matters more in a book-length project than a short document, since a bad revision pass can otherwise be hard to undo cleanly. You're capped at 40 named versions per document, and a toggle in the Version history panel lets you filter the list down to just the ones you named.

troubleshooting.problem: The document outline or table of contents skips a chapter
troubleshooting.cause: That chapter's title wasn't given a heading style, or got left on Normal text by accident.
troubleshooting.fix: Select the heading text and reapply the style through Format, then Paragraph styles.

troubleshooting.problem: Page Break in the Insert menu doesn't seem to do anything
troubleshooting.cause: The document is set to pageless format, which drops fixed margins and page breaks entirely.
troubleshooting.fix: Switch back to pages format from File, then Page setup, before inserting the break.

troubleshooting.problem: A named version is missing from Version history
troubleshooting.cause: The "Only show named versions" toggle in the panel is filtering it out, or the document has hit its 40-named-version cap.
troubleshooting.fix: Turn off the toggle to see every autosaved version, or delete an old named version to free up a slot.

faq.question: How do I quickly jump between distant chapters?
faq.answer: Open the Document Outline sidebar from the icon in the top-left corner. It lists every heading and lets you click to jump straight to that section.

faq.question: Will the table of contents update automatically?
faq.answer: Yes, an inserted table of contents updates as you add, rename, or reorder headings throughout your manuscript. It's added from Insert, then Page elements, then Table of contents.

faq.question: Can I export my finished manuscript for publishing?
faq.answer: Yes. File, then Download, includes EPUB Publication alongside PDF and Word formats. EPUB is what most e-reader apps and self-publishing platforms expect, and it builds its chapter navigation from the same headings you used for the outline, which is one more reason to keep heading levels consistent.

faq.question: Does Google Docs save my progress automatically?
faq.answer: Yes, changes save automatically to the cloud, and named versions in Version history give you extra milestone checkpoints you can return to.

faq.question: Why do my chapters need consistent heading levels?
faq.answer: Mixing heading levels inconsistently across chapters breaks both the Document Outline navigation and the automatic table of contents.

verifiedNote: Click path and screens come from a recorded walkthrough of a real sample manuscript. Re-checked against Google's own Docs Editors Help pages in September 2026, which corrected two moved menu paths this guide previously had wrong: table of contents now sits under Insert, then Page elements (not directly under Insert), and naming a version runs through the Last edit button top right rather than a File, then Version History menu item. The pageless-format caveat on page breaks, the 40-named-version cap, and the native EPUB export were added from the same check.
